Talking Point: Ocarina Of Time Revolutionised The 3D Swordfight, But How Does The Remake Hold Up In A Vintage Year For Clashing Blades?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nintendolife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that forget the hubbub around Grand Theft Auto.
  • It has been revealed that onimusha: Way of the Sword broke free of parryslop with exciting, flexible and immensely satisfying katana combat.
  • Sources indicate that it makes it a funny time for The Hero of Time to step back into the fray.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that forget the hubbub around Grand Theft Auto. Big Walk? Big deal. It’s all noise designed to distract us from 2026’s real legacy: that it’s been one of the best years on record for video game swordfighting.

It has been revealed that onimusha: Way of the Sword broke free of parryslop with exciting, flexible and immensely satisfying katana combat. Blood of Dawnwalker’s directional combat recreated a scintillating sense of strike-and-counterstrike rhythm rather than asking players to hide behind defensive blocks. Then Phantom Blade Zero swans in with cinematic style and a dazzling flurry of wuxia sword strikes and somersaults.

Sources indicate that it makes it a funny time for The Hero of Time to step back into the fray. After all, the original N64 Ocarina of Time practically set the template for today’s sword-toting successors. Dark Souls, Onimusha, even Kingdom Hearts’ keyblade battles all follow in Link’s Kokiri bootprints.

Ocarina of Time famously defined the lock-on, circle strafing, and the basic choreography of action-game design. According to a 2011 Iwata Asks, that genre-defining 3D swordfighting had a charming origin story (after a fleeting moment where they considered making Ocarina of Time in first-person!). It came about thanks to a ninja show witnessed by co-director Toru Osawa and colleagues on a frankly enviable work excursion to the Toei Kyoto Studio Park.

According to recent reports, as Osawa remembered the Japanese period film reenactment, “a number of ninja were surrounding the main samurai, and one lashed out with a kusarigama [a sickle and chain weapon]. The lead samurai caught it with his left arm, the chain stretched tight, and the ninja moved in a circle around him.”.

Industry observers note that action choreography was the remaining problem for director Yoshiaki Koizumi. At that same ninja show, he spotted the action movie routine that helps Jackie Chan inexplicably survive every movie:.

“First, one attacks while the others wait. When the first guy goes down, the next one steps in and so on [...] Watching that show at the studio park was a clue toward solving that problem. Z-targeting flags one particular opponent, telling the other enemies to wait.”.

That impeccable logic meant Link was safe from being mobbed by Keese swooping from offscreen in all directions. It was such a sound design principle that it continues to underpin action games today. But I suspect modern players no longer need to be handled with Koizumi’s kid gloves. Judging by the remake, Nintendo agrees.

Consider how Nintendo changed N64 Ocarina’s Forest Temple’s ominous fight against two Wolfos. Lock on to one, its counterpart scampers obediently into the background. Not so for the remake! These newly terrifying fiends aren’t just tankier, swifter, and more aggressive: they’ll conduct somersaulting tag-team switchups at will so you’re left to deal with a full health bar – just like the Lizalfos duo.

Industry observers note that it’s a lesson not every Ocarina successor learned. The latest Onimusha’s greatest flaw comes from how closely its mobs follow the age-old formula. Attacking one at a time, queuing up a procession of theatrical wind-up animations makes them trivially easy for a supremely talented Mushashi to attack, deflect, or even decapitate with a well-timed Issen counter. Dawnwalker’s usually not much better, sending vampire Brencis’s lackeys after you in patient succession.

In comparison, I have to commend Phantom Blade Zero for its willingness to toss out Koizumi’s Law, never passing up an opportunity to give players a well-deserved backstabbing.

But the remake’s multitude of combat changes go far beyond footwork and newly aggressive enemies. For all its modernising under-the-hood changes, playing it still feels like entering a mystical parallel universe where Sekiro never happened. I’m back with sword and shield in hand, without a high-risk, high-reward parry ability.

In a recent development, even with its snappier, flashier but deeply familiar combat, it took some getting used to a gentler pace compared to more recent upstarts. I started my playthrough thoroughly parrybrained after spending nearly 100 hours playing Dawnwalker into Wolverine before finally catching up with Metroid Dread. When I returned to Hyrule, it was with fingers already twitching with anticipation at every incoming blow.

Shorn of a now-trendy stamina meter, the fact that locking on to an enemy automatically raises your shields reduces the jeopardy; when I get hit, it’s because I got greedy.

One problem: I was ready to parry but Link wasn’t. In fact, the remake felt close to playing Dark Souls using the almost obligatory sword-and-shield build (with a parry I never learned to use properly!). As our review rightly noted, it’s laudably true to the original game, not even touching The Wind Waker’s combat-geared flourishes like the jump-spin attacks that would follow five years later.

The result is combat that feels almost like a cautious game of chess. You bait a mistake or trigger a weakness before going for the stunlock. Shorn of a now-trendy stamina meter, the fact that locking on to an enemy automatically raises your shields reduces the jeopardy; when I get hit, it’s because I got greedy. It may no longer be dangerous to go alone, but at least we have a few tips to help up the ante – I just wouldn’t recommend a swordless run!

Sources indicate that along with the absent stamina and posture meters, Ocarina remake’s simpler combat blessedly ignores a more recent swordfighting innovation: light and heavy attacks. Generally, I can live without the added layer of combat timing fussiness the Soulslike dominion has given us. It also avoids the pitfalls introduced by Phantom Blade Zero, where single inputs translate into a continuous flurry of attacks that can feel unsatisfyingly disconnected from the buttons I’ve pressed.

That’s not to say I wouldn’t say no to all modern embellishments. I’d love a high-powered combo finisher such as Wind Waker’s. But don’t forget: Ocarina already had a more entertaining means to deal a slow wind-up finishing blow capable of leaving its victim in a 6ft deep crater. It’s big, it’s bad, it’s the same height as your dad: it’s the Biggoron Sword!

But no matter the size of the sword he wields, Link’s return from the past has the vibe of a strangely youthful veteran checking in on his proteges. Musashi, Coen, and Soul are the new kids on the block, but they learned everything they know from their green-tunicked, rosy-cheeked master.

And if it ever comes down to a showdown, those newcomers simply aren’t getting past Link’s guard when he hasn’t got a stamina meter to wear down.

Capcom has today revealed that its dinosaur PvPvE shooter Exoprimal will end service on September 29, 2027, meaning it will no longer be playable after that date. The game is also set to be delisted from digital storefronts, including the Xbox Store, on March 30, 2027.

"We regret to announce that service for Exoprimal will be discontinued as of 8:00 PM (PDT) on Wednesday, September 29, 2027.".

Exoprimal launched on Xbox Series X|S on July 14, 2023, and suffered a pretty pants opening with only 4,995 players logging in through Steam to play Capcom's new team-based shooter.

Here's a detailed breakdown of what is going to happen to Exoprimal in the months leading to end of service:.

Following Capcom's mighty 2026 releases, Resident Evil Requiem and Onimusha: Way of the Sword, I wanted to understand what went wrong for Exoprimal, so I hopped back on. Funnily enough, I was actually enjoying the game, despite it being a ghost town. Only nine players were active at the time, and it really felt like it. It's still a fun title though, which makes the end of service announcement quite sad, at least for me.

GTA 6 is great because of all its murderous NPCs, not in spite of them

  • So I pull up to the side of the road, ready to head in and start my mission, when seemingly out of nowhere the four-wheeler comes barreling in, almost taking me out completely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it's come to my attention that some of us aren't having a very fun time with the NPCs in Grand Theft Auto 6. I've seen videos and threads of players complaining about not being able to steal cars because of crack head drivers, getting hunted down by killer NPCs, and just generally having a harder time traversing Leonida because who knows what bloodthirsty beast hides behind each corner? And to this I say, your steak is too buttery? Your lobster too juicy?

Recent findings suggest that my first interaction with one of the unfriendly residents of Leonida started when I accidentally bumped into their car. Because I am wholly unaware of my surroundings, I didn't even notice that anyone was mad at me as I listened to my pop songs and carried on driving towards my mission. Little did I know that right behind me was a four-wheeler with a driver who had steam coming out of her ears.

So I pull up to the side of the road, ready to head in and start my mission, when seemingly out of nowhere the four-wheeler comes barreling in, almost taking me out completely. The driver gets out and starts screaming about payback. I have no idea what I've done, but this is GTA 6, I'm not taking this slander. So I start swinging.

The fight ends with me knocking this lady out, but she doesn't go down without a fight. At one point, I actually thought that was it for me—taken out on the pavement by a soccer mum, what a way to go.

But even if I had taken a long sleep on the sidewalk, that would've been OK, because it's all part of the beautiful package that GTA 6 offers.

According to recent reports, I don't want vapid NPCs that buckle at the first sight of a handgun, or have the object permanence of a goldfish. Filling Leonida with some actually competent, and dare I say dangerous NPCs makes this game infinitely more interesting. I like not knowing how one small action will ruin my whole day, or having to be a little wary of the people around me lest I want to incur a murderous chase across the city streets.

Terrorising helpless NPCs is fun, but only for a short while.

I have a theory as to why players are pushing back against aggressive NPCs: they just don't like having to put in the effort after years of being able to do whatever they want in GTA Online. There's certainly some that will look back on the mostly timid NPCs of Los Santos and miss when all they had to do to steal a car was swing open its door and throw the limp driver out. Aside from shouting, there wasn't really anything a regular NPC could do to pose a threat to you back then.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Rockstar amped up the mayhem and carnage you could cause, turning it into a chaotic playground with few repercussions. GTA Online players have become accustomed to walking around like some vengeful god, wreaking havoc wherever or whenever they see fit, and only very occasionally dealing out mercy. Now these fickle deities have been forced to become human again.

Recent findings suggest that A part of me understands the appeal. Terrorising helpless NPCs is fun, but only for a short while. NPCs that actually have a backbone offer an experience that will keep me interested for far longer.

Plus, Leonida is based on Florida, do you honestly think you could terrorise the streets of Miami or Tampa Bay and walk out completely unscathed? Yeah, I thought as much.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I'm not sure I would've ever expected William Shatner to be mentioned in the same breath as Grand Theft Auto VI, but that's what's been happening as of late. A viral clip recently highlighted Shatner besmirching the recently released game, and it generated a bit of backlash. Now, Shatner is speaking out about the brouhaha. Frankly, I'm surprised the 95-year-old actor even knew what it was, and based on his latest comments, I'm still unsure whether he does.

It has been revealed that as Star Trek fans may be well aware, Shatner is relatively unafraid to offer an opinion on subjects he's not completely familiar with. He's landed in hot water before offering up tons of commentary on Trek, despite never watching the reveals, and now, a clip of him talking about the game on Piers Morgan Uncensored is making waves. The host prompted Shatner for his opinion on Grand Theft Auto VI, and he stated the following:.

No! I think it's the dumbest thing I've ever heard! Why don't you read a good book?

As one might expect, some people took offense to Shatner and other commentators' words on the program. This is, after all, a game that has made more than Taylor Swift's Eras tour in under a week. Comments on the clip popped up on X, and they were critical of all involved:.

The comments called out various claims, mainly the assertion that Grand Theft Auto VI is simply a "pimp simulator." Of course, it was previously revealed that the game would not allow prostitution, which was featured in previous releases.

According to recent reports, william Shatner seemed to catch wind of the negative comments and was quick to respond on his personal X account. He wanted to say that his comments were not meant to be inflammatory to the game or gamers, but rather to the four panelists that he had to sit and watch before doing his own segment:.

It has been revealed that last week there were a bucketful of nasty replies on this video clip where most of the angry “children” took the quote as a general statement but didn’t bother to see what I was referring to as ridiculous. Prior to my segment, there was a segment on GTA. Look at these 4 that got airtime 👇🏻! 🙄 Unfortunately, they probably don’t know how to read, especially the guy in 🕶️. That’s who they got to represent gamers. That’s what the comment was about. I had to suffer watching them it was ridiculous! 😤😑.

I'm hoping Shatner isn't stressed about this, because I know I'm not personally concerned about what opinion he holds on Grand Theft Auto VI. In fact, I would expect most people north of 90 years old would not be too interested in video games and would sooner read a book.

What I am interested in, however, are William Shatner's thoughts on past co-stars and what he has to say about space and life in general. Fortunately, he's often doing that as well as making frequent trips around the world to talk to anyone who will listen about his past feuds and time in Hollywood.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Grand Theft Auto VI is available to purchase right now, and William Shatner is frequently on the web offering up his opinion. I'm honestly still tickled that this whole situation even happened, and I love it when two pieces of pop culture I love intersect in an unexpected way.

Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Industry observers note that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of major ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more promptly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs noted, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

It has been revealed that here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 rolled out at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, Fresh Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

Industry observers note that in fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox customers in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the Newly introduced Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:.

Amusingly, Fresh Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first.".

Some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#133048. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2419 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • Industry observers note that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've noted it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

Industry observers note that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

According to recent reports, the problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a major, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to patch the image. Like I stated, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

Sources indicate that I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of key ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

Sources indicate that the "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Sources indicate that pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

Recent findings suggest that for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

Sources indicate that all of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a upcoming player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

Indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Recent findings suggest that both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

According to recent reports, in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the upcoming PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint matter in bright ambient light.

If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the latest RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Industry observers note that just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

According to recent reports, anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of problems like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Sources indicate that really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, right now, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

It's battery-powered, which means you can take it anywhere with you (as long as you have wifi). The battery lasts up to 1.2 hours for projecting video (in Eco Mode), and up to four hours as a speaker (it has built-in dual 3W JBL speakers). The auto keystone from XGIMI is one of the best ones I've experienced among all of the projectors I've tested, and it will adjust to practically any surface you cast it on, which can, with the 160° adjustable built-in stand, even be the ceiling. The current bundle brings an 80-inch screen included in the price.

If you have a bit more money to splurge, the MoGo 4 is the same concept as the Vibe One but takes its specs to the next level, and it's available starting at $359 (originally $499). It's still small and compact with 1080p resolution, but it nearly doubles the brightness, with 450 ISO lumens. The battery life more than doubles to two and a half hours in Eco Mode, while still keeping the projector under three pounds. It also has Google TV as its OS, but the projection is 360° with its adjustable built-in stand. You also have the option of getting the bundle with the PowerBase Stand, which extends the battery to five hours. Like the Vibe One, it has a built-in speaker, but this one uses dual 6W Harman Kardon speakers with Dolby Audio.The MoGo 4 Laser is a slightly upgraded version that uses triple laser technology for a better picture. It still supports 1080p resolution, but it's brighter with 550 ISO lumens and a 1000:1 contrast. The battery life, OS system, stand, speakers, and auto keystone technology are the same—but the bundles are different, so they're worth considering if they fit your needs.

If you're looking for a premium portable projector, the Horizon 30 Pro is a great option that competes with the best options on the market. It supports 4K resolution, uses RGB triple laser brightness that reaches 4800 ISO lumens (bright enough to see during the day), has a 120Hz refresh rate and gaming features to make gaming smooth, displays an 8,000:1 native contrast to make colors and blacks pop, and supports IMAX Enhanced, Dolby Vision, and HDR10+. It has an adjustable stand like the other XGIMI projectors and its own dual 12W Harman Kardon speakers with DTS Virtual:X and DTS-HD. The auto keystone is just as powerful as the other options, but the lens adds an optical zoom and a Lens Memory feature, which lets you save up to six custom lens and image setups and recall them with a click. Right now, it's down to $1,899 (originally $2,499) after a 24% discount.

Four years ago (oh my god) strategy RPG Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga rather impressed our reviewer Jon Bolding. He wrote that "novel tactical mechanics make this indie a contender for the best strategy RPG this year".

Well, buckle up, 2027, because Symphony of War 2 has broken cover with a promise to release next year, and it's coming courtesy of the strategy sommeliers at publisher Hooded Horse, which I take as a very good sign.

According to recent reports, SOW2 looks set to continue the Fire-Emblem-ish framework of its predecessor, tasking you with recruiting a gaggle of heroes to wage war with (and possibly compose symphonies, who's to say?) in "a world filled with political intrigue, betrayal, and tense, large-scale tactical battles". Which is a lot like our world, really.

It has been revealed that it all looks very nice indeed. In the announcement trailer, we get glimpses of its squad-based combat and anime cutscenes, and I am officially into both. The art is poppy and distinctive, at some point an age-of-sail warship transforms into some kind of German WW1 destroyer, and the overworld triggers the regions in my brain devoted to thinking about Heroes of Might and Magic. Check, check, and check.

Industry observers note that "Anime cutscenes!?" I hear you cry. "That sounds like the kind of thing that bespeaks a dense tapestry of lore I'll need to get to grips with first!" Well, apparently not. I am informed by Symphony of War 2's Steam page that the devs have no expectation you know what a "Nephilim Saga" even is before you pick this game up. "Symphony of War 2 is a standalone experience set several generations after the events of the first game—it can be enjoyed without having played Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga". The game's tale of a fallen empire trying to un-fall can be enjoyed single-serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ubisoft has confirmed more layoffs as part of its previously announced operational "reset", this time affecting 166 employees at its major Montréal and Québec City studios - the teams responsible for game series including Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. It indicates the cuts are necessary "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.".

GamesIndustry.biz reports the cuts - believed to equate to around four percent of the studios' total headcount - will impact employees working on projects either recently cancelled or significantly changed.

The publication also understands the cuts, remarked to primarily impact production and support roles at Ubisoft Montréal and Québec City, include members of Vantage Studios - Ubisoft and Tencent's joint development venture announced last October, which focuses on the publisher's biggest franchises, including Far Cry, Rainbow Six Siege, and Assassin's Creed.

In a statement provided to Eurogamer, Ubisoft confirmed it is, "reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations", adding: "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

Recent findings suggest that "We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues," the statement continued. "We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources.".

Industry observers note that these latest job cuts are part of a "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" announced by Ubisoft in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

BioWare turned down KOTOR 2 because LucasArts wanted the RPG done in 18 months

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (459 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gamesradar

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BioWare made one of the most beloved RPGs of all time with Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, but it was Obisidan that followed up with Knights of the Old Republic 2: The Sith Lords, another massively popular game.
  • Talking to Pembridge TV, Winski claims LucasArts approached BioWare to develop Knights of the Old Republic 2 and asked for the project to be completed in just 18 months.
  • Try, Obsidian did, and for the most part, it succeeded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BioWare made one of the most beloved RPGs of all time with Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, but it was Obisidan that followed up with Knights of the Old Republic 2: The Sith Lords, another massively popular game. It's somewhat well-documented that publisher LucasArts wanted the sequel done swiftly and that BioWare turned down the project for that reason, but in a upcoming interview, BioWare veteran John Winski confirms that's the case and even puts an exact number on LucasArts' request.

Talking to Pembridge TV, Winski claims LucasArts approached BioWare to develop Knights of the Old Republic 2 and asked for the project to be completed in just 18 months. "When LucasArts came to us and said, 'hey, you want to make a sequel?' We were like, 'OK,' and they gave us 18 months, and we were like, 'nope. No. We can't do it in 18 months. That's not enough time'," says Winski. "And then Obsidian was like, 'we'll try.'".

Try, Obsidian did, and for the most part, it succeeded. Winski rightfully points out Knights of the Old Republic 2 was released in a pretty sorry state, or in his words, not "totally finished," but he acknowledges that "a lot of people really love it" despite an "unreasonable" development cycle set by LucasArts. "It's still something that is worth having been done," he adds.

It really is remarkable how successful Obsidian was in following up such a celebrated release, and the very first RPG adaptation of Star Wars, with a game almost equally as beloved, all under pressure from the rights holder to deliver in an incredibly short timeframe. Just a couple of years later, the studio managed a similar feat with the release of Neverwinter Nights 2, yet another acclaimed RPG sequel to a BioWare-developed title. Leave it to Obsidian, I suppose.

Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic director isn't worried about pressure from RPG fans since his team already made KOTOR and Mass Effect: "We're not trying to fill someone else's shoes".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only been out for a matter of hours, and players have already tracked down a UFO in the woods and a Bigfoot in the swamps.

According to recent reports, the UFO encounter is a random night-time event in Kelly County, on a dirt road near the Starlet Motel safehouse east of Port Gellhorn. You'll need to have finished the game's first chapter, and it's most reliable after 2am in-game.

Recent findings suggest that as word spread late yesterday (18th November), it seems the event will kick off if you find a car at the side of the road with its headlights flickering, its trunk open, and clothes strewn around it. Follow the trail into the trees towards a blue glow, and you'll catch a UFO beaming down on a woman before it drops her and flies off. Head back to her car, as she requests, and the UFO returns for you. You apparently black out and come round three days later, and a bronze trophy called The Truth Is Out There should unlock.

You can seemingly trigger the event as either Jason or Lucia, and it isn't needed for 100 percent completion.

It has been revealed that and that's not the only close encounter you can expect, either. YouTuber Lazarbeam bumped into Bigfoot on the afternoon of 18th November, hours before the game introduced in the UK, while one Reddit user reported that they weren't quite sure what they'd stumbled on, titling their post "I think I found Bigfoot".

Sources indicate that leonida's version of Bigfoot is actually the Skunk Ape, Florida's own swamp cryptid, and it can be found in the swamplands near Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County as soon as free roam opens up. Listen out for a loud roar, then use Jason's tracking ability to follow it through the swamp. You may find it feeding on a deer carcass, while a second sighting has been reported south of Watson Bay.

Either way, the trail seemingly ends at a strange, human-like tree. Investigate it, and Jason blacks out, triggering a short cutscene in which the creature creeps up on him, as shown in this video. He later wakes near his vehicle, drenched in sweat. Save your ammo, though, as shooting at it won't do you any good.

Cryptids and aliens are, of course, something of a Rockstar tradition by this point. GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery kept players hunting for years, and Output Lag has already spotted two NPCs in a GTA 6 bar talking about goings-on there. Nobody has cracked a full Chiliad-style puzzle in the new game yet, but I'm sure that's just a matter of when, not if.

GTA 6 launched today on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, although some have been getting in on the action earlier as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even Latest Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first.".

According to recent reports, eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

The game is already available to pre-order on the Xbox Store at a low price of £21.99 / $24.99, and it also seemingly comes with Xbox Play Anywhere support (meaning you get a free PC copy too).

We'll leave you with more details on Arizona Sunshine below, launching for Xbox on January 21st of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives.
  • In a recent development, probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria.
  • There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

In a recent development, probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

Industry observers note that you lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

In a recent development, the game's New York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

Back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

According to recent reports, I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's New York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

"Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever!".

  • It has been revealed that the game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going big on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed company unveiled the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

It has been revealed that the game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

"I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura.".

Other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was confirmed that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

In a recent development, still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide shows up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. Then again, he's been very busy posting important things about the situation with Jensen Huang and Nvidia lately, so maybe he hasn't noticed.

It has been revealed that yes, the last post I've linked there is the Sweens giggling at an AI image of him, Huang, Johan Andersson, and John Carmack as the heads carved into Mount Rushmore that he himself asked Grok to generate. As you do.

We've got quite a few interesting Xbox releases still to come in December, and one of them that we've been keeping a close eye on is Stage Tour, which is a fresh Guitar Hero / Rock Band style game launching on December 10th.

They're not messing around with this one either, having snagged loads of famous bands for the tracklist, which now stands at well over 70 songs. There are going to be 90+ by the time we get to release, so there's more to come.

Let's take a look at all the confirmed songs so far:.

Stage Tour is at the moment available to pre-order on the Xbox Store at a price of £31.49 / $35.99 (with Xbox Play Anywhere support included), but obviously that assumes you already have an instrument to play the game with, such as the Riffmaster that we reviewed last year.

You'll also find hardware being sold alongside the game at various retailers, with the game and guitar bundle retailing at £119.99 here in the UK. There's also a drum kit, and band kit, and much more on the official Stage Tour website.

I'm personally just planning to stick with the Riffmaster and see whether Stage Tour can do enough to hold my attention amidst the likes of Rock Band 4, Clone Hero and YARG across console and PC, and I'm particularly intrigued by the "all-new roguelite Tour Mode" that apparently makes for an endlessly replayable campaign.

It has been revealed that let's see how it goes, eh? We'll try and bring you some hands-on coverage of Stage Tour ASAP.

Will you be playing Stage Tour on Xbox this December? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game introduced, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site. This latest leak appears to be making good on a threat posted back in October, where the group stated its intent to release a full, playable build of the game.

Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB. Eurogamer has seen the site and can confirm this is what the group has claimed, however I have been unable to verify the existence of any actual files. On the site, CyberLeek claims this build is from November 2026 - meaning it is very close to (if not the actual) release build. The 'executable file appears to be missing from the build, however, meaning you cannot actually - yet - get it up and running. CyberLeek is threatening to release this file at a later date, however.

Industry observers note that "It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads. "[Cyberleek] holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto 6, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one. The main executable is held on a countdown." CyberLeek states the executable will be released earlier than planned if its crypto token reaches a predetermined value. Many of the leaks to date have been related to a CyberLeek crypto scheme. Previously, it was estimated that the group cashed out at least £200,000.

What does all this mean? There's a very realistic chance that the game could be up and running on PC soon - undercutting Rockstar's unannounced PC release by a matter of months, if current rumours are to be believed. "This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps," the statement continues. "[CyberLeek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons.

"If the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds, [CyberLeek] will work to get a PS5 build - a fallback, most likely never required. Either way: the Xbox build is going out. No double dipping for Take-Two/Rockstar." It seems these are not empty threats.

Recent findings suggest that cyberLeek has been a thorn in Rockstar's side for a while now. The group initially claimed it took this action in the name of "Gamers' Rights", supposedly fighting for consumers in relation to the controversial discontinuation of game-discs and the digital-only future being pursued by game publishers. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity.

  • Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the firm.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

In a recent development, "Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft noted in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources.".

In a recent development, ubisoft Montreal are right now working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

Industry observers note that ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

It has been revealed that meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

Here is an incredibly far-off release date you can pencil in (and then probably rub out because it'll be delayed again): the wild and wacky Showa American Story is coming to PS5 on 28th October 2027.

It was originally planned to launch in 2026, so this is a pretty substantial delay to the game, but the "core game content" is now complete, according to the developer.

The next 11 months will be dedicated to "polishing and optimizing the experience so that when you step into Showa American Story, it feels cohesive, responsive, and complete".

For those who don't know, Showa American Story is based on the scenario where "Japan has bought out most of the United States with its strong economic power. A surge of immigration has firmly planted Japanese culture within the American continent. Two cultures are rapidly amalgamated, although conflicts are inevitable, citizens gradually adapt to a life never imagined as time goes by.".

Sources indicate that this leads to a bizarre adventure, which we got a small taste of at Gamescom earlier this year. You play Chigusa Choko, a female movie star brought back from the dead who sets out on a quest with vibes of Shenmue, Yakuza, and No More Heroes.

What we played was incredibly unfinished and janky, but there was still some promise on show. Let's hope almost a year of polish and further work on the game turns it into a strong experience.

Can you wait that long to play Showa American Story? Let us know in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just a day after Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek released the executable for the near-complete Xbox build of the game they dropped on Friday, at least two of the leads of Leonida, the biggest and best-known effort to recompile it to run on PC, have called it quits—seemingly under pressure from Take-Two and Rockstar.

Recent findings suggest that the release of the exe made the pirated Xbox build effectively complete, and that opened the door for recomp projects to do their thing—that is, to leverage AI to quickly whip up a version of the game that will run on PC. Some hackers estimated it could be done within a week; Shayder, one of the lead developers on the Leonida project, said on X that followers could "expect a lot of static recompilation work to be done soon.".

In a separate message on the Leonida Discord, Shayder tempered expectations a bit, writing that "it will take at least a week" to come up with something playable on PC. During a subsequent livestream, however, the team was seemingly able to get the GTA 6 splash screen to come up on PC, although it crashed after that. It sure seemed like things were moving ahead quickly.

Recent findings suggest that but then things began moving promptly in a different direction. "I quit guys. I’m sorry," NotRexed, apparently the head of the project, posted last night on X. "I really want to make cool stuff but every single time shit happens that I can’t control so I’m stepping away. Thank you everybody, especially in the discord that allowed me to have this opportunity.".

It has been revealed that later, they added, "Last post from me. I wanna clear things up. Rockstar taking my server down was only part of the reason. Like I’ve remarked before, I’m a 15 year old kid. Managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on Discord. Goodbye.".

Shayder, who had previously predicted rapid progress on the Leonida effort following the release of the Xbox executable, took a more direct approach and simply deleted all of their X posts.

Keep up to date with the most key stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

According to recent reports, this isn't necessarily the end of work to bring GTA 6 (in a probably not-great state) to PC via AI. Other such projects are underway, and there also appears to be an effort to carry on with Leonida: The website remains up, with a latest name attached as owner, and there's at least one Discord server dedicated to it, although it appears a little less focused at this point than the original Leonida server. A new Github repository (NotRexed also deleted that) has been set up: It's "a continuation of NotRexed's Leonida project," according to a note on the project, which adds that "development continues here with its full commit history.".

Recent findings suggest that the advent of AI greatly simplifies and speeds up the work of bringing console games to PC (as long as you're not too picky about the quality), and that makes life tougher for companies that want to keep a lid on such projects. Still, it's not surprising that Take-Two and Rockstar are going hard on it: In the past, Take-Two has moved aggressively to shut down GTA 5 mod projects, an effort that culminated in its acquisition of the biggest and best of them. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.
  • Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet said mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.
  • According to recent reports, "Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.

Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet said mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.

According to recent reports, "Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said. "Today, we can say that console and PC remain our core focus for our biggest franchises.".

He added: "The focus is really to make sure that we come with strong growth on console and PC, and notably PC, which is a more dynamic platform than ever.".

Sources indicate that ubisoft last confirmed its China-set mobile game was still in the works in March, when it was mentioned in the publisher’s Assassin's Creed: Into 2026 blog. Assassin's Creed now sits within Vantage Studios, Ubisoft's joint venture with Tencent, which introduced last year.

Sources indicate that ubisoft's results also confirmed some more changes to the way the company is run, with the publisher saying its new operating model is "now fully in place". Creative Houses 3 and 5 have been combined under the leadership of Julien Bares "to leverage synergies between Live experiences across platforms".

All leadership roles across the Creative Houses are now filled, too. An external general manager has been appointed for Creative House 4 and is set to join in January 2027, though Ubisoft hasn't yet confirmed who. That follows September's appointment of 2K and Amazon Games veteran Christoph Hartmann to lead Creative House 2, home to The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell, which was renamed Massive Entertainment at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that outside the Creative Houses, Motherbrain, the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI experiment Teammates, is now a subsidiary in its own right. It's working on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds". A separate unit has also been set up to look after brands that don't belong to any of the Creative Houses.

Ubisoft says the upcoming structure is already paying off, pointing to the commercial success of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and renewed momentum for Rainbow Six Siege, which it says ranked among the top 10 games across Xbox and PlayStation for monthly active owners over the half.

That mentioned, the publisher nonetheless posted a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half of the year, with net bookings down 16.5 percent to €644.7 million.

Sources indicate that the news comes just hours after Ubisoft confirmed 166 job cuts at its Montréal and Québec City studios, the latest in a year of layoffs. They're part of the "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" that Ubisoft revealed in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

In a recent development, since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

On the weekend, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on a new Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it was unveiled that Robert Pattinson had been cast as James Bond, Twilight fans everywhere did a little cheer.
  • First off, in case you missed it, James Bond is brought up around 58 minutes into 2008’s Twilight.
  • Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw https://t.co/eMfeaVhbhuNovember 16, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it was unveiled that Robert Pattinson had been cast as James Bond, Twilight fans everywhere did a little cheer. Especially if you were Team Edward! What a good long-term investment that’s turned out to be! However, the most popular Twilight-related reaction to Pattinson being 007 stems from the fact that the iconic spy was brought up in the vampire movie. As it turns out, there’s a whole newly introduced layer to that scene we didn’t know about.

First off, in case you missed it, James Bond is brought up around 58 minutes into 2008’s Twilight. Just seconds before Edward Cullen and Bella Swan make their grand entrance as a couple for the first time at school, one of their classmates, Eric, hands out flyers for the upcoming prom, which is a Monte Carlo theme. Check out the scene below:.

Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw https://t.co/eMfeaVhbhuNovember 16, 2026.

Industry observers note that isn’t that wild? James Bond is literally stated in Twilight right before the current James Bond appears. However, there’s more to it. The movie’s director, Catherine Hardwicke, revealed something latest about the scene while talking about the casting on The Kyle Buchanan Show. In her words:.

I remarked, ‘Let’s put the sunglasses on that day,’ and he got out of the car and he looked so suave that he inspired the line Bond, James Bond… Justin kind of ad-libbed it. It’s kind of cool because we did think he looked like James Bond. So, I guess we were seeing the future.

That happened 18 years before it became a reality. I guess it goes to show the role has been right for Robert Pattinson all along given those on the set of Twilight were thinking about it, too. Pattinson didn’t earn the role easily, either. All sorts of other eligible actors such as Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden reportedly auditioned for Denis Villeneuve’s film. Charlie Cox also recently mentioned he was shot down for being “too old” even though he’s just three years older than Pattinson.

Hardwicke certainly had a hand in making Pattinson the significant name he is. And, while talking about the actor, she recalled what stuck out about him when he auditioned for Twilight. In her words:.

He’s intense, and he’s interesting, and he’s got a lot of stuff going on in there, and he’s weird and he’s original. He doesn’t fit the mold and he’s not scared to think or say crazy shit, which is what I love about him.

While it’s perhaps a bit surprising Amazon MGM Studios didn’t opt for an actor who was an unknown, Jeff Bezos has stated that in the screen tests it was “so obvious” Pattinson was their Bond that they didn’t dare pick anyone else. We can’t wait to see what his Bond will be like, and given his career thus far, it sounds like it might be unexpected.

Sources indicate that while we wait for Bond 26, you can get excited to see Robert Pattinson in Dune: Part 3 on December 18. Oh, and the whole Twilight saga is there for anyone with a Netflix subscription.

Keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Industry observers note that each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

In a recent development, gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today! If you're interested in doing so, you can pick it up on Steam right here.

Blizzard wants to "get rid" of best-in-slot items in World of Warcraft: Forever by introducing situationally strong gear
